newsitem.title: UK: Soyinka says he expected Nigeria treason charges. [CORRECTED 17:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Soyinka says he expected Nigeria treason charges. [CORRECTED 17:45 GMT]

text.p: Exiled Nigerian opposition leader and Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka said on Wednesday he was not surprised to be charged with treason because it was clear Nigerian leader Sani Abacha wanted to "eliminate" him.
Nigeria's military government on Wednesday charged Soyinka and 11 others with the capital offence of treason over recent bomb blasts on army buses which killed three soldiers.

"We learned the decision to try us on treason charges had been taken before the recent violence...The whole thing is orchestrated. Abacha is trying to get rid of us," Soyinka said by telephone from California.
"Abacha is intensifying his attempts to eliminate us. He is heading towards sentencing us to death in absentia. This is what he's gunning for. This is why we have been charged with treason," he said.
Soyinka, who won the 1986 Nobel Prize for Literature, is a leading opponent of Abacha and has consistently accused him of smothering democracy in the populous west African state.
Nigeria has been in crisis since 1993 when the army annulled an election to restore democracy.

Soyinka and some of those charged with him are fighting for the annulment to be reversed and for Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the vote, to be freed and installed as president. Abiola was jailed in 1994 (corrects from 1944) when he declared himself president.
Relations with the West plunged to a new low in November 1995 when Nigeria executed author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists after they were convicted of murder.
"Abacha has taken this decision to put a judicial face on what he's decided to do to us," said Soyinka.

The radical playwright and novelist, who fled to Europe and the United States more than two years ago, strongly condemned the country's rulers in a 1996 book entitled "The Open Sore of a Continent: A Personal Narrative of the Nigerian Crisis".
One of those charged is Anthony Enahoro, leader of the exiled wing of the opposition National Democratic Congress (NADECO), who said he was surprised by the treason charges.
"Abacha knows no other way of dealing with the opposition than eliminating them," he said by telephone from Virginia, denying that NADECO had been involved in the bombings.
"I don't see how (the charges) will answer the argument that he is not the legitimate president of Nigeria."

Other accused Nigerians include Frederick Fasehun, president of the Campaign for Democracy pressure group, and former finance minister Olu Falae. "I don't know who is behind the bombs. He's created so much enmity in the army that I think the army could be responsible. It is very divided," said Soyinka, adding that it would be some time before the situation in Nigeria changed.
"The dissent in Nigeria has been there from the very beginning and will not go away until Abacha has gone. But this is a marathon, not a sprint."
